titleStmt.title: Interview with Mary Ester Asher, Undated
titleStmt.author: William M. Gibson

projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Mary Ester Asher was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: This is Bill Gibson with United States Senator Richard Lugar's office. And today we are interviewing Mary Esther Asher. She was born on May 4th, 1912. She currently resides at [address redacted], in Greenwood, Indiana, 46143, and her telephone number is [number redacted]. She served in the Navy as part of the Navy Nurse Corp, and achieved the highest rank of lieutenant commander during the World War II time. Her primary dates of enlistment were from July 1943 to around February 1946. Ms. Asher, thank you very much for being here. The first thing we always ask is how did you end up in the Navy, and how did you end up in the Nurse Corp?

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: Well, of course I was already a nurse, a pediatric nurse at Winchester, Virginia. And it was war time, and, you know, they were sort of encouraging everybody to join, and I preferred the Navy.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: Now, at the time, do you remember how your family reacted to you joining and what they thought of you going into the service in the Navy?

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: Well, they really didn't say very much.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: Good luck.

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: Now, when you joined the Navy where did you go? You were in Winchester, Virginia as a pediatric nurse. Where did they send you in the Navy.

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: My first duty station was the naval hospital in Seattle.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: And do you remember what that was like when you got there and how that might have been different from the type of nursing and type of duties you were doing in civilian life?

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: One of the things they ask you is in what field of nursing have you had previous experience. Well, at that point during the war they were taking care of dependents in the military. And before that I had worked in the psychiatric hospital. And first they had a psychiatric department, and that's where I wound up, on the lock ward. And so many of the fellows resented being in the service, and they didn't get along with their officers, and so they would be sent, you know, for psychiatric evaluation. Well, it was the point you didn't know who was psychiatric and who wasn't.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: How long were you there and doing those duties?

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: Well, I wasn't in the psychiatric ward all the time that I was there, but that was my first assignment. I was on a variety of other wards. And I'd say 12 to 16 months I was there? And --

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: What -- Go ahead.

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: And I think 12 of us were sent down to Schumacher, California.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: And that was, you know. And we were at the dispensary there.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: And what were your duties when you were there? What position did you hold, or did you move up the ranks at all at that point?

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: Well, that's when I became lieutenant commander, while I was there. And it was just general nursing, you know, there at the dispensary.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: And then I think it was, you know, January, February of '46, everybody was getting out, so I was discharged but remained in the Navy Reserve.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: Now, you had said something before we started the interview about doing some, some work with air transportation; is that right, with the patients?

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: I guess that was my first before I went to --

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: Seattle?

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: -- Schumacher.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: Okay. Now, what did you do there?

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: On board ship?

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: Yeah. What was -- Kind of what were the duties?

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: Well, we were on call most the time. We had sick call in the morning, and then there were two nurses on the ship, and one of us would be on call the rest of the day. And, of course, we were just there to -- because of the dependents on the ship. And I remember making all these baby formulas. And one day -- We made the formula in one room, and then the refrigerator where they were kept were in the next room. Well, aboard ship, you know, between each room it's a step up to get out, you know --

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: -- into get in to the passageway. And this one day it was really rough at sea, and trying to fill those baby bottles like this, you know. I had quite a struggle. And the other nurse was taking the rack around to put it in the refrigerator. And she was one of those individuals, if one hair was out of place, it was a calamity, you know. Well, she fell with all of those bottles, and she said all I was interested in, was did the bottles break. I wasn't interested in whether she was hurt or not. But that was one thing that I remember particularly.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: How long did you have to serve on the ship, do you remember?

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: Over a year.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: Over a year.

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: I don't remember.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: Now, you said you also said you took a number of trips to Alaska?

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: Well, that was when I was aboard ship.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: Oh, going from Seattle to Alaska and back?

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: I was up there, the longest and the shortest day of the year that particular year. When was it? It was 1950 or something like that.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: And I remember one time and we went in the wintertime up there, to -- the ice breaker had gone in ahead of us to -- but when we got to the pier, they could only get the bow of the ship to the pier because if they took the ship over to the pier, the ice would have taken the pier out. So the people that got off there had to get off at the bow of the ship.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: Now, were there any interesting soldiers that you met during this time, any people in the Navy, the guys that served in the Navy that left a particular impression on you during your time there?

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: Well, I have corresponded at Christmastime with several ever since then, but, of course, father time's played a part in that now, and fewer and fewer.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: But there was a few in the Navy that I still correspond with at Christmastime.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: That's wonderful. How many would you say you corresponded with when the first few years that you were out? How many do you think that you were still corresponding with at that time?

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: Well, I'm sure it was more than a dozen.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: As I say there's not very many of them now.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: Made a lot of good connections then?

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: What did you do after your military service? Did you stay in the nursing field?

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: Um-hum. My first job after I got out last time was Culver Military Academy.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: And did you marry or have any children or anything?

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: No, I never married.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: Now, you'd said after the World War II time you stayed in the reserves, and then were you called back to active duty at any point?

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: Not after the time that I was in during the Korean War. After the Korean War I got out and I was never called anymore.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: When did you get out of the duty from the Korean War? Do you remember when that was?

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: I think it was' 67.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: You said you'd been called to duty for that around 1950 or do you remember when you were called to duty for that?

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: After all this time I can't remember all those dates.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: I understand. Now, the duty that you served for the Korean War was still out in California and Seattle area, out west; same sort of duty that you served in World War II?

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: First it was the military sea transportation first. And then after that it was the east coast. I was stationed in Portsmouth, Virginia, in Annapolis, Maryland, and Chelsea, Massachusetts, and Key West.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: That's a variety. Now, are there any other stories that were particularly interesting or memorable for you from your time in the military, your time serving as a nurse there?

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: Nothing particular, you know, on the east coast. I remember I especially didn't want to go to Key West. And I don't know whether you've ever been to Key West or not.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: I haven't.

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: Well, from the main land of Florida down to the first town was a pretty desolate area, and I swear, I would have stopped to the side of the road and cried but there was no place to pull off the road, so I had to keep going. But, you know, I really enjoyed my duty in Key West, but there wasn't much there. We all had to make our own fun, you know.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: And I was there at the time of the Russian invasion into Cuba.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: The Cuban missile crisis?

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: Um-hum. I was there at that time. That's when my family was concerned about me.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: Were you equally concerned or did you feel fairly okay?

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: It didn't bother me too much, but the one funny experience I had while I was there. There's a beach along the east coast. And I was driving, and there was an area that was enclosed in barbed wire fence, and the missiles pointed to Havana and so forth. And just outside the fence there was a couple lying there sunbathing, lying practically up against the fence. I was so sorry I didn't have my camera with me.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: That would have been a pretty funny sight. They apparently weren't too concerned.

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: Now, you got out. You stayed in nursing. You went to Culver Military Academy, and then what did you do after that?

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: Let's see.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: When you went to work for Culver Military Academy, is that the first time you'd moved back to Indiana before your duties in the service?

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: Yeah. That's the only duty that I actually ever had _____ as a nurse.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: Oh, okay. Where did you serve the majority of your time as a nurse after the war?

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: For the life of me I can't remember what I did after I left. I'm drawing a blank.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: Yeah. Where did you work the majority of your career after the war? Did you work in any particular location for a long period of time?

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: Let's see. I was discharged when I was stationed at Charleston, South Carolina. I'm sorry.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: That's okay. When did you finally retire from nursing? Do you remember when that was?

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: It was '67.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: Sixty-seven?

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: I was in Charleston then.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: Do you have any other interesting stories from your time in the military that you want to share today?

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: Well, Alaska was interesting, you know. Anchorage, which is really the southern part of Alaska, and in the shortest days the sun came up about 10 o'clock in the morning, and 2 o'clock the day was done. And the longer days you could -- Well, there's about two hours of darkness at night. And that trip that I -- the tour after, that was in July, and we went up to Fairbanks, and they said you could tee off on the golf course at midnight.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: It's never quite as warm up there, even in the summertime --

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: -- as it is elsewhere?

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: It's comfortable, but it never gets real hot, of course.

sp.speaker: William M. Gibson
sp.p: Well, I appreciate you taking time to be with us today, Mary. And we will make sure that this recording becomes a part of the Library of Congress record about your service and what you did. And thank you very much for your time.

sp.speaker: Mary Ester Asher
sp.p: You're welcome.
